question: Which of the following best defines real property?
choice_a: Any item that can be physically picked up and moved from one location to another
choice_b: Only the land itself, excluding any structures or improvements built on it
choice_c: Personal belongings located inside a dwelling
choice_d: Land and everything permanently attached to it, together with the bundle of legal rights that come with ownership
explanation: Real property consists of land, everything permanently attached to it (improvements and fixtures), and the bundle of legal rights of ownership (possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition). Personal property (chattel) is, by contrast, movable.
source_note: Real property vs. personal property distinction; the bundle of legal rights concept. Foundational national real estate principle.

question: A freestanding microwave that sits on a kitchen counter and can be unplugged and carried away without tools or damage to the home is generally classified as:
explanation: Items that are not permanently attached and can be removed without damaging the structure remain personal property (chattel) unless a contract states they convey with the real property.
source_note: Personal property/chattel classification, national principle.

question: When determining whether an item that was once personal property has become a fixture (and therefore part of the real property), the courts generally look at the method of attachment, the adaptation of the item to the property, the intention of the party who installed it, and any agreement between the parties. Which of the following is generally NOT part of this legal test?
choice_a: The method used to attach the item to the property
choice_b: The original purchase price the current owner paid for the item
choice_c: Whether the item was specially adapted for use with the property
choice_d: The intention of the person who installed the item
explanation: The fixture test focuses on method of attachment, adaptation to the real estate, intention of the annexor, and agreement/relationship of the parties. The item's original purchase price is not part of this legal test.
source_note: Fixture determination test (method, adaptation, intention, agreement), national principle.

question: A tenant installs custom display shelving and specialized equipment in a rented retail space solely for use in the tenant's business. Under the trade fixture exception to the general fixture rule, this equipment is treated as:
choice_a: Real property that automatically transfers to the landlord when the lease ends
choice_b: A permanent fixture that can never be removed under any circumstances
choice_c: Personal property that the tenant may remove before the lease ends, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage
choice_d: Jointly owned property split between landlord and tenant
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for the purpose of conducting business remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed, so long as the tenant repairs any damage caused by removal.
source_note: Trade fixture exception to the general fixture rule, national principle.

question: Ownership of real property is generally transferred by which legal instrument, while ownership of personal property is transferred by a bill of sale?
explanation: Real property is conveyed from grantor to grantee by deed; personal property (chattel) is transferred by a bill of sale.
source_note: Conveyance instruments for real vs. personal property, national principle.

question: A legal description that begins at a defined point of beginning (POB) and follows a series of compass directions (courses) and distances along the boundary of the parcel back to the point of beginning is known as:
explanation: A metes and bounds description defines a parcel's boundaries using courses (directions) and distances measured from a point of beginning, ultimately returning to that same point.
source_note: Metes and bounds legal description method, national principle.

question: A legal description that identifies a parcel by a specific lot number within a numbered block of a subdivision, as shown on a map filed with the county recorder's office, is known as:
choice_b: The lot and block (recorded plat) method
explanation: The lot and block (recorded plat) method identifies a parcel by its lot number, block number, and a reference to the recorded subdivision plat map.
source_note: Lot and block/recorded plat legal description method, national principle.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, the intersection of a principal meridian (a north-south reference line) and a base line (an east-west reference line) is used primarily to:
choice_a: Mark the exact center point of every individual section
choice_b: Define the point of beginning for a metes and bounds description
choice_c: Establish the reference point from which townships and ranges in that survey area are measured
choice_d: Set the boundary lines of a recorded subdivision plat
explanation: The rectangular survey system uses principal meridians and base lines as reference lines from which townships (measured in tiers north/south of the base line) and ranges (measured in columns east/west of the meridian) are located.
source_note: Government/rectangular survey system reference lines, national principle.

question: Under the government rectangular survey system, a standard township is a 6-mile by 6-mile square divided into how many sections?
explanation: A standard township is 6 miles square and is divided into 36 sections, each one mile square.
source_note: Government survey township/section structure, national principle.

question: A standard section of land under the government rectangular survey system contains how many acres?
explanation: A section is one square mile, which is equal to 640 acres.
source_note: Government survey section size, national principle.

question: One acre of land is equal to how many square feet?
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet. This is a standard land measurement conversion used throughout real estate practice.
source_note: Standard land measurement conversion (acre to square feet), national principle.

question: A rectangular room measures 14 feet by 18 feet. What is the square footage of the room?
explanation: Square footage is calculated as length multiplied by width: 14 ft x 18 ft = 252 square feet.
source_note: Standard structure area (square footage) calculation, national principle.

question: A lien that attaches only to one specific, identified piece of property, such as a mortgage on a particular home or a mechanic's lien for work done on a particular building, is called a:
explanation: A specific lien attaches only to a particular, identified property. A general lien, by contrast, attaches to all property owned by the debtor (for example, a judgment lien or estate tax lien).
source_note: Lien classification: specific vs. general liens, national principle.

question: As a general rule, the priority among competing liens against the same real property is determined by the order in which each lien was recorded, with one major exception: which type of lien typically takes priority regardless of its recording date?
explanation: Liens generally have priority in the order recorded ('first in time, first in right'). However, real property tax liens and special assessment liens typically have superior (first) priority regardless of when they were recorded.
source_note: Lien priority rules and the property tax lien exception, national principle.

question: A contractor who furnishes labor or materials to improve real property but is not paid may file which type of lien against that property?
explanation: A mechanic's (or materialman's) lien is a specific, involuntary lien that a contractor, subcontractor, or material supplier may file when not paid for work or materials furnished to improve real property.
source_note: Mechanic's lien concept, national principle.

question: An easement that benefits one parcel of land (the dominant estate), burdens an adjoining parcel (the servient estate), and automatically transfers with the land whenever either property is sold, is called an easement:
explanation: An easement appurtenant involves a dominant estate (benefited parcel) and a servient estate (burdened parcel) and runs with the land, automatically transferring to new owners of either parcel.
source_note: Easement appurtenant (dominant/servient estates), national principle.

question: A utility company's recorded right to run power lines across a private landowner's property, where the benefit belongs to the utility company itself rather than to another parcel of land, is an example of an easement:
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or company (such as a utility) rather than another parcel of land, and there is no dominant estate.
source_note: Easement in gross, national principle.

question: A property owner gives a neighbor oral, temporary permission to park a boat trailer in the owner's driveway for one week. This permission, which the owner may revoke at any time, is best described as a:
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable, and generally non-transferable permission to use another's land. Unlike an easement, it is not a permanent property right and does not run with the land.
source_note: License vs. easement distinction, national principle.

question: A neighbor's fence is mistakenly built two feet over the property line onto the adjoining owner's land. This type of unauthorized physical intrusion onto another's property is called a(n):
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement (such as a fence, wall, or roof overhang) extends onto an adjoining owner's property without permission. Encroachments are typically discovered through a survey.
source_note: Encroachment concept, national principle.

question: A person who occupies another's land openly, notoriously, continuously, exclusively, and without the owner's permission for a statutory period of time may eventually be able to claim legal ownership of that property through the doctrine of:
explanation: Adverse possession allows a non-owner who occupies land openly, notoriously, continuously, exclusively, and hostilely for a statutory period to potentially obtain legal title. Even an unresolved or potential adverse possession claim can create a cloud on title.
source_note: Adverse possession as a potential encumbrance on title, national principle.

question: When a property owner dies, real property owned by that person often must pass through a court-supervised process that validates the will (if any) and formally transfers title to the heirs or beneficiaries before a sale can be completed. This process is called:
explanation: Probate is the court-supervised legal process of administering a deceased person's estate, including validating a will and transferring title to heirs or beneficiaries. An open or unresolved probate matter can delay or complicate the marketability of title.
source_note: Probate as a potential encumbrance affecting marketable title, national principle.

question: A property is sold while an existing tenant still has time remaining on a signed lease. From the new owner's perspective, that existing lease is best understood as:
choice_a: An encumbrance that limits the new owner's right to immediate possession of the property
choice_b: A lien that must be paid off in full at closing
choice_c: An easement appurtenant that benefits the new owner
choice_d: A deed restriction imposed by local government
explanation: A lease creates a leasehold interest in favor of the tenant, which encumbers the property by limiting the new owner's right to immediate possession until the lease term ends or is otherwise lawfully terminated.
source_note: Existing lease as an encumbrance on ownership, national principle.

question: An owner conveys the surface of a parcel of land to a buyer while retaining ownership of the coal, oil, and gas located beneath the surface. The retained interest is known as:
explanation: Mineral rights (subsurface rights) can be severed from surface ownership and retained, leased, or conveyed separately from the surface estate.
source_note: Severance of mineral/subsurface rights from surface ownership, national principle.

question: The legal right to use, control, and occupy the space above a parcel of land, which can be sold, leased, or developed separately from the surface (for example, to allow construction of an overhead structure), is known as:
explanation: Air rights are the rights to use and control the airspace above a property and, like mineral rights, can be severed and transferred independently of the surface estate.
source_note: Air rights concept, national principle.

question: The doctrine giving an owner of land bordering a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream, the right to reasonable use of the adjacent water is known as:
explanation: Riparian rights apply to land bordering flowing water such as rivers and streams. Littoral rights apply to land bordering non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes and oceans. Prior appropriation is a separate doctrine, used mainly in arid western states, that allocates water rights based on permit and beneficial use rather than land adjacency.
source_note: Water rights doctrines: riparian, littoral, and prior appropriation, national principle.

question: When a single person or a single legal entity owns real property in their own name with no co-owners, this form of ownership is called ownership in:
explanation: Severalty ownership means the property is owned by one person or entity alone, 'severed' from co-ownership by others.
source_note: Severalty (sole) ownership, national principle.

question: Two co-owners hold title to a property with unequal ownership shares. Upon the death of one co-owner, that owner's share passes to their heirs rather than automatically to the surviving co-owner. This describes:
explanation: Tenants in common may hold unequal ownership shares, each has an undivided interest in the whole property, and there is no right of survivorship — a deceased tenant's interest passes to that tenant's heirs or estate.
source_note: Tenancy in common characteristics, national principle.

question: For a valid joint tenancy to be created at common law, the co-owners generally must acquire their interests with the same four unities, traditionally identified as:
explanation: The traditional four unities required for a joint tenancy are unity of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (acquired by the same document), interest (equal ownership shares), and possession (equal right to use the whole property).
source_note: Joint tenancy: the four unities requirement, national principle.

question: The feature that most clearly distinguishes joint tenancy from tenancy in common is:
choice_a: The requirement that co-owners be married to one another
choice_b: The ability of co-owners to hold unequal ownership shares
choice_c: The requirement that the property be held through a business entity
choice_d: The right of survivorship, under which a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s)
explanation: Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship: when one joint tenant dies, that tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing probate. Tenancy in common carries no right of survivorship.
source_note: Right of survivorship in joint tenancy, national principle.

question: A special form of co-ownership available only to married couples in many states, which includes a right of survivorship and generally cannot be severed or conveyed by only one spouse acting alone, is:
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership for married couples that includes a right of survivorship and generally requires both spouses' consent to convey or encumber the property.
source_note: Tenancy by the entirety, national principle.

question: In a condominium form of ownership, an owner holds fee simple title to their individual unit and, together with the other unit owners, holds an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the:
choice_a: Units individually owned by the other owners
choice_b: Common elements, such as hallways, grounds, and shared structural components
choice_d: Proprietary lease covering the entire building
explanation: Condominium owners hold fee simple title to their individual unit and an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements, in addition to membership in the condominium association.
source_note: Condominium ownership structure, national principle.

question: In a housing cooperative, a resident typically does not hold title to real property directly. Instead, the resident owns:
choice_a: A fee simple deed to their individual unit
choice_b: A life estate in the entire building
choice_c: Shares in the corporation that owns the building, together with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
choice_d: A timeshare interest in multiple units
explanation: In a cooperative, the corporation holds title to the entire building. Residents own shares of stock in the corporation and receive a proprietary lease granting occupancy rights to a specific unit.
source_note: Cooperative ownership structure, national principle.

question: An arrangement in which multiple buyers each purchase the right to occupy a property, such as a vacation unit, for a designated recurring period each year is known as a:
explanation: A timeshare divides use, and sometimes ownership, of a property among multiple parties, each holding rights to occupy the property during a specific recurring time period.
source_note: Timeshare ownership form, national principle.

question: When real property is held in trust, legal title is held by the ______, who manages the property according to the trust document for the benefit of the ______.
explanation: In a trust arrangement, the trustee holds legal title and manages the property according to the trust instrument for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds equitable title.
source_note: Ownership held in trust, national principle.

question: When a property owner dies without having transferred title before death, the real property is managed and eventually distributed by an executor or court-appointed administrator as part of the deceased's:
explanation: Upon death, a decedent's real property becomes part of the estate, administered by an executor (if named in a will) or an administrator (appointed by the court if there is no will) until distributed to heirs or beneficiaries.
source_note: Ownership by/through a decedent's estate, national principle.

question: When real property is owned by a corporation, title is generally held:
choice_a: By each shareholder individually as tenants in common
choice_b: By the corporate officers as joint tenants
choice_c: In the corporation's own name as a distinct legal entity, in severalty
choice_d: Automatically in trust for the benefit of the shareholders
explanation: A corporation is a distinct legal entity that can hold title to real property in its own name, in severalty, separate from its individual shareholders.
source_note: Ownership by business entities (corporations), national principle.

question: An ownership interest that entitles the holder to possess and use a property only for the duration of their own lifetime, after which the property passes to another designated party, is called a:
explanation: A life estate grants ownership and use rights that are limited to the lifetime of the life tenant. Upon the life tenant's death, the property passes to the holder of the remainder or reversion interest.
source_note: Conventional life estate ownership, national principle.

question: A deed creates a life estate for one person and names a specific third party who will receive full ownership of the property once the life tenant dies. That third party's future interest is called a:
explanation: A remainder interest is a future interest granted to a third party (someone other than the original grantor) that becomes possessory when the life estate ends. If the property instead reverts to the original grantor or the grantor's heirs, rather than to a named third party, that future interest is called a reversion.
source_note: Remainder vs. reversion future interests following a life estate, national principle.
